title: Three Common Sleep Habits Are Silently Ageing Your Brain. A 23,000-Person Study Just Identified Them.
excerpt: Sleeping too little, napping too often, and struggling to fall asleep were each independently linked to white matter damage — a marker of dementia risk.
body:
A study of more than 23,000 middle-aged and older adults has identified three common sleep habits that are independently linked to accelerated brain ageing — and two of them are behaviours that millions of people consider harmless, or even healthy.

The research, published in the journal *Alzheimer's & Dementia*, tracked participants from the UK Biobank who completed detailed sleep questionnaires and then underwent MRI brain scans roughly nine years later. The scans measured white matter hyperintensity volume — areas of damage in the brain's wiring that accumulate with age and are strongly associated with cognitive decline, stroke, and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.

## The Three Habits That Stood Out

The University of Arizona team, led by graduate researcher Madeline Ally and senior author Gene Alexander, initially examined five sleep behaviours: sleep duration, daytime napping, sleeplessness, unintentional daytime dozing, and snoring. All five showed initial links to greater white matter damage. But after adjusting for smoking, physical activity, blood pressure, and vascular health conditions, only three remained significant.

**Sleeping outside the 7-to-9-hour window** was the strongest signal. People who reported sleeping fewer than seven hours per night had measurably larger volumes of white matter lesions than those who slept within the recommended range. The researchers noted that short sleep appeared more damaging than long sleep, though they cautioned that more data on habitual long sleepers is needed.

**Frequent daytime napping** was the second independent risk factor — a finding likely to surprise the many people who view afternoon naps as a wellness practice. While short naps can boost alertness and mood, the study found that habitual napping was associated with greater signs of brain ageing. The questionnaire did not distinguish between a twenty-minute power nap and a two-hour afternoon collapse, so the researchers acknowledged that nap duration and timing may matter.

**Sleeplessness — difficulty falling or staying asleep** — was the third. Chronic insomnia can reduce the quality of restorative deep sleep, when the brain performs critical functions including waste clearance through the glymphatic system, memory consolidation, and cellular repair.

"Sleep is a universal but complex behaviour, and there is still much to learn about how different aspects of sleep relate to brain health," Ally said. "What our findings suggest is that these behaviours are not interchangeable — each one makes its own distinct contribution to vascular brain health."

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

The findings carry particular weight for South Asian communities, where several cultural and lifestyle factors conspire against healthy sleep.

Intergenerational households — common across the Indian diaspora — often mean disrupted sleep schedules, with grandparents rising early for prayers and younger family members staying up late. Frequent long-haul travel between the US and India, with its brutal twelve-and-a-half-hour time difference, imposes repeated circadian disruption. And a 2024 study in *Scientific Reports* found that young South Asians in the UK had significantly higher daily sitting times and lower physical activity than white Europeans — both factors that can degrade sleep quality.

There is also the cultural normalisation of napping, particularly among older adults. Afternoon naps are a deeply embedded habit across South Asia, and the finding that frequent napping correlates with brain ageing — independent of other risk factors — is a genuine wake-up call.

Dr. Samir Fahmy, director of the Sleep Disorder Center at NYC Health + Hospitals, offered practical advice. "The emphasis should shift from 'how to sleep better at night' to 'how to structure your day to optimise sleep,'" he said. He recommends waking at the same time every day, getting natural light within the first hour, exercising in the late afternoon, and following a structured wind-down routine of thirty to sixty minutes before bed.

## What You Can Do

The study's most hopeful implication is that sleep is a modifiable risk factor. Unlike genetics or age, the three behaviours identified here are things people can change. Keeping sleep duration within the seven-to-nine-hour window, being mindful about daytime napping, and addressing sleeplessness through behavioural interventions like cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) could all help protect the brain's white matter as it ages.

For a community that faces elevated cardiovascular and metabolic risk even while reporting healthier diets and lower alcohol consumption, sleep may be the overlooked variable that ties part of the puzzle together.
